summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Clark County and Nevada foster children stated clearly established substantive due process claims under the 'special relationship' doctrine for inadequate safety and medical care, and the court applied the Blessing test to determine which Child Welfare Act and CAPTA provisions are privately enforceable under § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: Frames agency liability where a child in care suffers serious harm.
key_cases.quote: Having examined the relevant contours of a foster child's clearly established due process rights to adequate safety and medical care

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a State to protect a child from private violence it did not create, even where the agency received repeated abuse reports and failed to act. (Joshua DeShaney was never in state custody and survived with profound brain injury; this is not a death-in-care case.)
key_cases.relevance: The starting point for analyzing agency responsibility for serious harm to a child, and the reason the custody exceptions matter.
key_cases.quote: its language cannot fairly be extended to impose an affirmative obligation on the State to ensure that those interests do not come to harm through other means.

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21 (voluntary Extended Young Adult Support Services Program). A “young adult” is a person at least 18 but less than 21 years of age who either (1) on his or her 18th birthday was subject to a court order for placement in foster care or was the subject of proceedings held pursuant to NRS 432B.410 to 432B.590, inclusive, of which placement in foster care is a potential outcome, or (2) exited the Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program established pursuant to NRS 432B.622 or an adoption assistance program after attaining 16 years of age and is not currently receiving care from his or her guardian or adoptive parent (NRS 432B.5915). To be eligible to participate the young adult must enter into a written agreement with the agency which provides child welfare services, must be enrolled in a program of secondary education or a GED-equivalent program, enrolled in a program of postsecondary or vocational education, enrolled or participating in a program or activity designed to promote employment or remove obstacles to employment, employed at least 80 hours per month, or incapable of satisfying any of those requirements due to a documented medical or cognitive condition, and must make a good faith effort to achieve the goals set forth in the plan developed pursuant to NRS 432B.595 (NRS 432B.594(1))

Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
